blocks.content: There is an old joke in software engineering that there are only two hard problems: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors. The joke works because it is true. Deciding when a cached value is no longer good enough to serve sounds like it should be simple, and in the easy cases it is, but the hard cases touch nearly every other topic in this section: consistency, replication, distributed cache clusters, and the CAP theorem all show up the moment invalidation has to work correctly across more than one machine.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281738533-152832259.png
blocks.alt: Cache invalidation earns its reputation honestly, it sits at the intersection of almost every other hard distributed systems problem

blocks.content: 1. What Cache Invalidation Actually Means

Invalidation is the act of telling a cache that a value it is holding is no longer trustworthy, either because the underlying data changed, or because enough time has passed that it might have changed. Get this wrong in one direction and users see stale, wrong data. Get it wrong in the other direction and the cache barely helps at all, because everything gets thrown away the moment it might conceivably be out of date.

The word "invalidation" covers a few genuinely different mechanisms, expiring after a fixed time, actively removing an entry the moment its source changes, and actively updating an entry in place, and picking the right one for a given piece of data is most of what this topic is actually about.

It helps to be precise about scope, too. Invalidation can happen at the level of a single key (one user profile changed), or at the level of an entire category (every product in a category had its price adjusted). Getting the granularity right matters a great deal, since invalidating too broadly throws away perfectly good cached data along with the genuinely stale piece.
1.1 A quick mental model

Picture a whiteboard with a sticky note on it. The sticky note is the cache entry, and the whiteboard underneath is the real data. Invalidation is simply deciding when the sticky note might no longer match what is written on the board, and either peeling it off (delete), writing new information on top of it (update), or setting a timer that peels it off automatically (TTL). Every technique on this page is a variation of one of those three moves.
2. The Core Tension: Freshness vs Performance
blocks.text: 2. The Core Tension: Freshness vs Performance

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281740996-477413012.png
blocks.alt: Invalidating aggressively keeps data fresh at the cost of cache effectiveness; invalidating rarely keeps the cache fast but risks staleness

blocks.content: Every invalidation strategy is really a position on one spectrum. At one end, invalidate the instant anything might have changed, and the cache stays perfectly fresh, but also barely reduces load on the database, since it gets thrown away almost as fast as it gets filled. At the other end, invalidate rarely or never, and the cache is maximally effective at absorbing load, but users can end up looking at data that quietly stopped being true a while ago.

Neither extreme is usually correct. The right answer depends entirely on the data: a stock price and a user profile picture have wildly different tolerances for staleness, and a good design treats them differently rather than applying one blanket policy everywhere.

It helps to name this trade-off explicitly for each piece of data during design, rather than discovering it by accident in production. A product price and a product description, sitting in the very same database row, often deserve completely different invalidation treatment once you actually think about how each one is used downstream.

This is also why a single blanket cache TTL applied across an entire application, a common shortcut in a first implementation, tends to age poorly as a system grows, different data genuinely needs different answers to this question, and treating them all the same eventually shows up as either unnecessary staleness somewhere or unnecessary cache misses somewhere else.
3. TTL-Based Expiration
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521158-262378383.png
blocks.alt: The simplest approach: a cached value automatically expires after a fixed amount of time, no matter what

blocks.content: The simplest invalidation strategy needs no coordination with the data source at all: attach a time-to-live (TTL) to every cached entry, and once that time passes, treat the entry as gone, forcing the next request to refetch from the source of truth.

SET user:42:profile "{ ...serialized profile... }" EX 300
# expires automatically after 300 seconds (5 minutes)

code.content:
SET user:42:profile "{ ...serialized profile... }" EX 300
# expires automatically after 300 seconds (5 minutes)

codes.text:
SET user:42:profile "{ ...serialized profile... }" EX 300
# expires automatically after 300 seconds (5 minutes)

blocks.content: The appeal is real simplicity: no invalidation logic to write, no events to publish, just a number. The cost is equally real: for up to the full length of the TTL, a stale value can be served to users with no way for the system to know it has become wrong sooner than that.

TTLs also interact with the thundering herd problem covered in depth under Cache Stampede: if a very popular key expires and a large number of concurrent requests all miss at once, they can all rush to the database simultaneously. That specific failure mode, and its fixes, belongs to that topic, but it is worth knowing the two problems are closely related.
3.1 Jittering TTLs to avoid synchronized expiry
blocks.text: 3.1 Jittering TTLs to avoid synchronized expiry

blocks.content: A subtle refinement worth knowing: if many keys are all set with the exact same TTL at roughly the same time, they all expire at roughly the same moment too, creating a burst of simultaneous cache misses. Adding a small amount of random jitter to each TTL, expiring in 300 seconds plus or minus a random 30 seconds, spreads that expiry out over time instead of letting it land all at once.
4. Write-Through Invalidation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281745778-462603455.png
blocks.alt: The application updates the cache in the very same request that writes to the database, so the two never fall out of sync

blocks.content: A more active approach updates the cache at the exact moment the underlying data changes, in the same logical operation as the database write itself. This keeps the cache continuously fresh rather than relying on time passing, at the cost of every write now doing two things instead of one, and needing to handle the case where the cache update succeeds but something else in that same operation fails, or vice versa.

Write-through invalidation trades a small amount of write latency (the cache update itself takes a little time) for a much smaller staleness window than TTL alone provides. For data where users would actually notice staleness quickly, a shopping cart total, an inventory count during a flash sale, that trade is almost always worth making.
4.1 Using Change Data Capture instead
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521158-63013782.png
blocks.alt: Rather than the application remembering to update the cache, a change data capture stream watches the database directly and triggers invalidation automatically

blocks.content: A more robust variant avoids relying on application code remembering to invalidate the cache on every single write path (easy to forget when a new code path is added later). Instead, a Change Data Capture (CDC) stream watches the database write-ahead log directly and emits an event for every change, which a dedicated consumer turns into cache invalidation. This decouples "did the data change" from "did every engineer remember to invalidate the cache," which is a meaningfully more reliable guarantee at scale.
5. Delete vs Update: A Real Design Choice
blocks.text: 5. Delete vs Update: A Real Design Choice

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281749291-565286598.png
blocks.alt: Updating a cache entry risks it briefly disagreeing with the database; deleting it forces a clean refetch on the next read

blocks.content: When a write happens, there are two ways to handle the existing cache entry: update it to the new value directly, or delete it and let the next read repopulate the cache from the database. Updating sounds more efficient, why make the next reader pay for a fresh database read when you already have the new value in hand, but it is quietly more dangerous: if two writes race each other, it is possible for an older write to finish second and overwrite the cache with stale data, leaving the cache and the database disagreeing indefinitely.

Deleting is safer specifically because it removes the possibility of that race entirely, the next read is always forced to go to the source of truth, guaranteeing the cache converges back to correct. Most production systems default to delete, reserving update-in-place for situations where the extra database round trip is specifically too expensive to accept.

blocks.title: A concrete rule
blocks.content: When in doubt, delete rather than update. A cache miss followed by a fresh read is always correct. An update done in the wrong order is a bug that can sit undetected for a long time.

["Delete-on-write: safe by default, costs one extra read on the next cache miss.","Update-in-place: saves that extra read, but only safe when writes to a given key are guaranteed to be strictly ordered."]
items: Delete-on-write: safe by default, costs one extra read on the next cache miss.
Update-in-place: saves that extra read, but only safe when writes to a given key are guaranteed to be strictly ordered.

blocks.content: 6. Event-Based Invalidation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281751011-877674965.png
blocks.alt: A write publishes an event, and every cache subscribing to that event clears the affected key, wherever it happens to be running

blocks.content: In a system with multiple cache instances, or multiple services that each maintain their own cache of the same underlying data, a single write cannot directly reach every cache that might be holding a stale copy. The common fix is publishing an invalidation event onto a message queue or pub/sub channel the moment a write happens, and having every interested cache subscribe to that channel and clear the affected key the instant the event arrives.

This is the same publish/subscribe pattern covered under the Fanout Pattern topic elsewhere in this course, applied specifically to the problem of keeping many independent caches in sync with a single source of truth.

This approach also scales naturally to invalidating a CDN edge cache, exactly the same event, "this piece of content changed," can trigger a CDN purge API call as one more subscriber alongside the application-level caches, unifying invalidation logic across every layer described in the next section rather than maintaining separate ad hoc invalidation code for each one.

It is worth choosing the transport for these events deliberately. A lightweight pub/sub channel (Redis pub/sub itself, or a dedicated topic on a message broker) is usually sufficient, since invalidation events are small and transient, there is little value in the durable, replayable guarantees a full event log like Kafka provides for this specific use case, though nothing prevents using one if it is already the standard infrastructure choice elsewhere in the system.
7. Invalidating Across Multiple Cache Layers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281752552-672005994.png
blocks.alt: A single data change may need to be invalidated at the local cache tier, the shared cache tier, and a CDN edge tier all at once

blocks.content: Real systems often cache the same data at more than one layer at once, a local in-process cache, a shared Redis cluster, and possibly a CDN edge in front of all of it. A single data change needs to be reflected at every one of those layers, not just the nearest one, or a user can end up seeing three different versions of the truth depending on which layer happened to answer their request.

Skipping a layer is an easy mistake to make precisely because it fails silently, everything looks correct in testing (where a developer usually only has one cache layer running locally) and only surfaces in production, where the full multi-layer stack is actually present.

A practical habit that helps here: whenever a new cache layer is added anywhere in a system, immediately go back and check every existing invalidation path to confirm it now covers the new layer too, rather than discovering the gap later through a confusing bug report.
8. The Race Condition Hiding in Plain Sight
blocks.text: 8. The Race Condition Hiding in Plain Sight

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281754192-74304387.png
blocks.alt: A read that started before a write commits can re-populate the cache with a stale value right after the write already tried to clear it

blocks.content: Here is a subtle failure that catches teams off guard: a write invalidates (deletes) a cache entry, but a read that was already in flight, one that fetched the old value from the database just before the write committed, finishes afterward and repopulates the cache with that now-stale value. The invalidation happened, and the cache went stale again anyway, moments later, through no fault of the invalidation logic itself.

The most common mitigation is a short "hold-off" delay before a read is allowed to repopulate the cache after any recent write to that same key, giving the write enough time to fully settle before the cache is trusted to accept new entries again for that key.

This exact race is why some teams prefer to invalidate slightly after a write commits, adding a small deliberate delay, rather than invalidating in the same instant, trading a few milliseconds of guaranteed staleness for eliminating the race window entirely.

Some teams instead solve this by having the write path itself perform the final cache write, rather than trusting whichever read happens to run last, removing the race by removing the ambiguity about which operation gets the final say over what the cache should hold.
9. Stale-While-Revalidate
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281756015-264188407.png
blocks.alt: Rather than blocking on a fresh fetch the moment a TTL expires, serve the stale value immediately and refresh quietly in the background

blocks.content: An increasingly popular middle ground: the moment a TTL expires, instead of making the next unlucky request wait on a full fresh fetch, serve that request the stale value immediately, and kick off a background refresh at the same time. The next request after that gets the freshly updated value, and no single user ever experiences the full latency of a cache miss.

This approach originated in HTTP caching (it is a real Cache-Control directive browsers understand natively), but the same idea applies just as well inside an application cache, and is worth reaching for any time a request would otherwise have to pay the full cost of a synchronous refresh on every single expiry.
9.1 An alternative: versioned cache keys
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281757575-937472909.png
blocks.alt: Rather than invalidating an old value, simply start writing to a new key, letting the old one quietly expire on its own

blocks.content: A different trick sidesteps invalidation entirely for certain kinds of data: instead of updating or deleting a key when the underlying data changes, encode a version into the cache key itself, and simply start writing to the new versioned key going forward. The old version is never actively invalidated, it just stops being read, and eventually expires naturally via its own TTL. This works especially well for data that changes in clearly defined versions rather than continuously, a configuration file, a compiled asset bundle, a machine learning model.
10. Choosing an Invalidation Strategy

["Ask how quickly staleness becomes a real, noticeable problem for this specific piece of data.","Ask how many independent places cache this same data, one service, or several.","Ask whether the write path is fully within your control, or whether data can change through a path invalidation logic cannot see."]
items: Ask how quickly staleness becomes a real, noticeable problem for this specific piece of data.
Ask how many independent places cache this same data, one service, or several.
Ask whether the write path is fully within your control, or whether data can change through a path invalidation logic cannot see.

blocks.content: 10.1 Getting the granularity right
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785281759294-532944577.png
blocks.alt: Invalidating too broadly wastes a perfectly healthy cache; invalidating precisely only what changed keeps the rest of the cache useful

blocks.content: A common, costly mistake is invalidating an entire cache region because one piece of data inside it changed, rather than targeting just the affected key. Precise, fine-grained invalidation keeps the rest of an otherwise healthy cache intact, which matters enormously at scale, where "just clear everything and let it repopulate" can translate into a genuine, painful spike in database load.
11. Common Mistakes

["Choosing update-in-place for convenience without considering the write-ordering race described in §5.","Forgetting a secondary cache layer (a CDN, a local instance cache) exists at all, and invalidating only the most obvious layer.","Setting TTLs based on a guess rather than the actual tolerance for staleness that specific data has.","Not handling the in-flight-read race condition from §8, then being confused when a cache \"randomly\" goes stale again right after being cleared."]
items: Choosing update-in-place for convenience without considering the write-ordering race described in §5.
Forgetting a secondary cache layer (a CDN, a local instance cache) exists at all, and invalidating only the most obvious layer.
Setting TTLs based on a guess rather than the actual tolerance for staleness that specific data has.
Not handling the in-flight-read race condition from §8, then being confused when a cache "randomly" goes stale again right after being cleared.

blocks.content: A less obvious mistake worth naming: invalidating a cache entry without confirming the write it depended on actually committed successfully. If a database transaction rolls back after the cache was already cleared in anticipation of it succeeding, the cache correctly ends up empty, but the next read repopulates it with the same old value the invalidation was meant to replace, at the cost of one wasted round trip. Rarely dangerous, but worth understanding as a real, if minor, inefficiency.
Treat every one of these as a checklist item during design review specifically, not just something to fix reactively once a real staleness bug is reported by a confused user.
12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: A strong answer here goes straight to the freshness-versus-performance tension rather than immediately naming techniques, since that tension is the actual reason this problem is hard in the first place. From there, being able to explain why delete is generally safer than update, and naming a real mitigation for the in-flight-read race, shows a level of depth well past a memorized definition.
Cache invalidation is hard not because any one technique is complicated, but because getting it wrong is silent, a stale value looks exactly like a correct one until someone notices it is not.

It is also worth being ready to discuss a real example from experience if one exists, invalidation bugs tend to be memorable precisely because they are so quiet, and a real anecdote about a stale cache causing a confusing production issue often lands better than a purely theoretical answer.
Key Takeaways

["Cache invalidation is fundamentally a trade-off between data freshness and cache effectiveness, not a single correct technique.","TTL-based expiration needs no coordination but can serve stale data for the entire length of the TTL.","Deleting a stale cache entry on write is generally safer than updating it in place, since deletion cannot leave the cache and database silently disagreeing.","Event-based invalidation is necessary the moment more than one cache instance or service needs to stay in sync with a single source of truth.","A subtle race between an in-flight read and a recent write can re-introduce staleness moments after an invalidation already ran.","Stale-while-revalidate serves a stale value immediately while refreshing in the background, avoiding making any single user pay for a slow cache miss."]
items: Cache invalidation is fundamentally a trade-off between data freshness and cache effectiveness, not a single correct technique.
TTL-based expiration needs no coordination but can serve stale data for the entire length of the TTL.
Deleting a stale cache entry on write is generally safer than updating it in place, since deletion cannot leave the cache and database silently disagreeing.
Event-based invalidation is necessary the moment more than one cache instance or service needs to stay in sync with a single source of truth.
A subtle race between an in-flight read and a recent write can re-introduce staleness moments after an invalidation already ran.
Stale-while-revalidate serves a stale value immediately while refreshing in the background, avoiding making any single user pay for a slow cache miss.

blocks.title: How this connects to the rest of this section
blocks.content: Cache Stampede covers what happens when many requests miss at once, often right after an invalidation. Cache Consistency covers the deeper question of how much staleness a system can tolerate in the first place, which is really the policy question invalidation strategy exists to implement.

A closing way to think about this entire topic: invalidation is not a single mechanism to memorize, it is a policy decision made once per kind of data, and every technique on this page is simply a tool for implementing whatever policy that data actually deserves.
